attributes.nuance_translation: A fairly formal way to say that something must not be done.

attributes.body:
てはいけない is used in Japanese to express that (A) 'cannot', or 'must not' be done. It is the combination of a verb in て form, the は particle, and the negative potential form of 行（い）く (to be able to go). In this way, it literally means '(A) cannot/is not able to go'.

Although は can be dropped from many phrases and expressions, the は in this particular grammar point is usually not. This is because いけない would then become the second action in a sequence of events (the usual function of て form). However, to make this more casual, ては is often changed to ちゃ (ては becomes ちゃ), or じゃ (では becomes じゃ), as this is easier to say.

Caution

Apart from いけない; ならない and だめ are also frequently used to get across the same meaning. However, they are used in different situations.

いけない - Fairly neutral. Used in both spoken and written language.

ならない - Fairly formal. Used mostly in written language.

だめ - Very casual. Used almost exclusively in spoken language.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: Something that must or must not be done
"HAVE TO", "NEED TO" "SHOULD HAVE", "I WISH...HADN'T" in Japanese
Prohibition: …ては + だめだ・いけない・ならない

attributes.body: Both てはいけない and てはならない express prohibition, saying something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. The two forms are equivalent in meaning, with the only difference being that ならない is slightly more formal and therefore more often found in the written language, such as in rules or regulations.

べからず and てはいけない are similar in that they both express prohibition, or the idea that you 'must not' or 'cannot' do something. The difference is in formality and how they connect to other words. べからず is a highly formal and archaic expression that nowadays is found mostly in regulations, proverbs, and so forth. It follows directly after the plain form of a verb, e.g. 入るべからず ('Do not enter.'). In contrast, てはいけない is far more common in the modern language, and connects to the て-form of verbs, e.g. 入ってはいけない ('You must not enter.')

first_relatable.title: べからず
first_relatable.meaning: Do not, Must not, Should not, Cannot (べからざる)

attributes.body: てはいけない expresses prohibition, meaning something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. In contrast, なくてはならない expresses obligation or something that 'must' be done. These forms can be tricky for learners, as the negative form なくてはならない (literally, 'it's not good if you don't') means 'must,' while the affirmative form てはいけない ('it's not good if you do') means 'must not.'

てはいけない expresses prohibition, meaning something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. In contrast, べきではない suggests that something 'should not' be done, often implying it's improper or that there's a better option. While both express negative recommendations, てはいけない is more authoritative and used for rules, whereas べきではない carries a more subjective nuance.

second_relatable.title: べきではない

attributes.body: てはいけない expresses prohibition, meaning something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. In contrast, なくちゃ and なきゃ are casual contractions of なくてはいけない and なければいけない, which express obligation—saying that something 'must' be done. The two forms differ in both formality (formal vs. casual) and meaning ('must not' vs. 'must').

なくてはいけない expresses necessity or obligation, something that 'must' be done. In contrast, てはいけない means something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. These forms can be tricky for learners: なくてはいけない looks negative but means 'must' (literally, 'it's not good if you don't'), while てはいけない looks affirmative but means 'must not' (literally, 'it's not good if you do').

なくてもいい means something is optional; 'it's okay not to (do something).' In contrast, てはいけない expresses prohibition; 'you must not' or 'cannot' do something. For example, 食べなくてもいい means 'It's okay not to eat it,' while 食べてはいけない means 'You must not eat it.' The first gives freedom; the second sets a rule.

てはいけない is used to express prohibition, meaning that something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. In contrast, なければいけない expresses obligation, something 'must' be done. These forms can be tricky for learners, as なければいけない is negative in form but means 'must' (literally, 'it's not good if you don't'), while てはいけない is affirmative in form but means 'must not' (literally, 'it's not good if you do').

てはいけない is used to express prohibition, meaning that something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. なければならない expresses the opposite meaning, i.e., that something 'must' be done. These forms can be tricky for learners, as なければならない appears negative but means 'must' (literally, 'it's not good if you don't'), while てはいけない appears affirmative but means 'must not' (literally, 'it's not good if you do'). (いけない and ならない themselves are essentially synonymous, though ならない is somewhat more formal/written-style.)
